claim: HP1E gene is a testis-restricted Drosophila HP1 paralog born more than 60 million years ago
source: The HP1E gene is a testis-restricted Drosophila HP1 paralog born more than 60 million years ago (Levine et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim cites a previous publication (Levine et al., 2012) as support for the evolutionary age and tissue restriction of HP1E

claim: HP1E localizes to developing spermatids subsequent to the completion of meiosis II
source: All three reagents revealed that HP1E localizes to developing spermatids subsequent to the completion of meiosis II (Figure 1A–C, Figure 1—figure supplements 2, 3, 4), ruling out a role for HP1E during the pre-meiotic or meiotic phases of spermatogenesis.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from three different reagents (Flag-tagged, YFP-tagged HP1E, and antibody) and multiple figures showing localization patterns

claim: HP1E signal was generally diffuse across a subset of the chromatin throughout spermiogenesis
source: HP1E signal was generally diffuse across a subset of the chromatin throughout spermiogenesis (Figure 1A–C)
evidence: The claim is supported by microscopy images showing HP1E localization patterns

claim: HP1E disappears completely at sperm maturation
source: HP1E signal was generally diffuse across a subset of the chromatin throughout spermiogenesis (Figure 1A–C) but disappeared completely at sperm maturation (Figure 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by microscopy data showing absence of HP1E signal in mature sperm

claim: HP1E disappearance in late spermiogenesis is not due to antibody inaccessibility in the highly condensed sperm head
source: Native expression of the HP1E-YFP fusion transgene confirmed our immunofluorescence results (Figure 1—figure supplement 4), implying that HP1E disappearance in late spermiogenesis is not due to antibody inaccessibility in the highly condensed sperm head.
evidence: The claim is supported by YFP fusion protein data that confirms antibody results, ruling out an alternative explanation

claim: HP1E localizes to paternal chromosomes only during the radical reorganization of histone-rich chromatin into protamine-rich sperm DNA
source: These data demonstrate that HP1E localizes to paternal chromosomes only during the radical reorganization of histone-rich chromatin into protamine-rich sperm DNA and disappears once sperm mature.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the timing of HP1E localization during spermiogenesis and its disappearance at maturation

claim: HP1E knockdown during spermiogenesis affects the expression of over 700 genes
source: We found that HP1E knockdown during this narrow developmental stage affects the expression of over 700 genes (fdr < 0.05, Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq data analysis

claim: 100% of significantly misregulated heterochromatin-embedded genes are upregulated when HP1E is depleted
source: However, one intriguing pattern that does emerge from this dataset is that 100% of significantly misregulated heterochromatin-embedded genes are upregulated when HP1E is depleted (Figure 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq data showing differential expression patterns

claim: Less than 60% of significantly misregulated euchromatin-embedded genes are upregulated when HP1E is depleted
source: In comparison, less than 60% of significantly misregulated euchromatin-embedded genes are upregulated.
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq data analysis

claim: The dichotomy between the effects of HP1E depletion on the euchromatic and heterochromatic compartment is highly significant (p < 0.00001)
source: This dichotomy between the effects of HP1E depletion on the euchromatic and heterochromatic compartment is highly significant (p < 0.00001)
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of RNA-seq data

claim: HP1E acts directly on the heterochromatic compartment
source: This dichotomy between the effects of HP1E depletion on the euchromatic and heterochromatic compartment is highly significant (p < 0.00001) and suggests a direct action of HP1E in the heterochromatic compartment, akin to its closest HP1 relative, HP1A (Kellum et al., 1995; Levine et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is inferred from differential gene expression patterns and comparison to HP1A function

claim: HP1E-depleted fathers produce highly penetrant male sterility
source: Both drivers efficiently knocked down HP1E expression (Figure 3—figure supplement 1) and both resulted in highly penetrant male sterility (Figure 3A).
evidence: The claim is supported by fertility assay data using RNAi knockdown

claim: A recoded, RNAi-resistant HP1E transgene fully rescued fertility of HP1E-depleted males
source: This recoded, RNAi-resistant HP1E transgene (Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 2) fully rescued fertility.
evidence: The claim is supported by rescue experiment data

claim: HP1E knockout males are completely sterile
source: We found that HP1E knockout males are also completely sterile, and this sterility is also fully reversed by the recoded HP1E transgene (Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by genetic knockout and rescue experiments

claim: HP1E is required for male fertility in D. melanogaster
source: Thus, HP1E is required for male fertility in D. melanogaster.
evidence: The claim is inferred from multiple genetic experiments showing sterility upon HP1E loss

claim: HP1E-depleted fathers produce abundant motile sperm that transfer to females, fertilize eggs, and initiate embryogenesis
source: Unlike the vast majority of male sterility mutants, HP1E-depleted fathers produce abundant motile sperm that transfer to females, fertilize eggs, and initiate embryogenesis (Figure 3B).
evidence: The claim is supported by microscopy data showing sperm production, transfer, and fertilization

claim: Embryos sired by HP1E-depleted fathers failed to hatch (0.5% hatch rate)
source: However, embryos sired by HP1E-depleted fathers failed to hatch (0.5% hatch rate).
evidence: The claim is supported by embryo viability assay data

claim: HP1E-depletion results in paternal effect lethality
source: These data demonstrate that HP1E-depletion results in PEL i.e., zygotic viability is dependent on father's genotype.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that embryos die despite successful fertilization

claim: Embryos fathered by HP1E-depleted males arrested after only a few rounds of zygotic mitosis
source: Embryos fathered by HP1E-depleted males ('PEL embryos' hereafter) arrested after only a few rounds of zygotic mitosis (Figure 3C)
evidence: The claim is supported by embryo staging data

claim: PEL embryos exhibited a chromatin bridge in the very first mitotic division
source: Embryos fathered by HP1E-depleted males ('PEL embryos' hereafter) arrested after only a few rounds of zygotic mitosis (Figure 3C) and exhibited a chromatin bridge in the very first mitotic division (Figure 4A).
evidence: The claim is supported by microscopy data showing chromatin bridges

claim: Aged PEL embryos exhibit increasingly asynchronous nuclear cycling and acute mitotic catastrophe
source: Aged embryos exhibit increasingly asynchronous nuclear cycling and acute mitotic catastrophe (Figure 4B).
evidence: The claim is supported by time-course microscopy data

claim: PEL embryos revealed no gross defects in maternal chromatin dynamics
source: PEL embryos revealed no gross defects in maternal chromatin dynamics (Figure 5A)
evidence: The claim is supported by microscopy data tracking maternal chromatin

claim: PEL embryos exhibited stereotypical centrosome and spindle morphology
source: PEL embryos revealed no gross defects in maternal chromatin dynamics (Figure 5A) and exhibited stereotypical centrosome and spindle morphology (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data of mitotic structures

claim: Sperm DNA in PEL embryos underwent the protamine-to-histone transition
source: Furthermore, sperm DNA in PEL embryos underwent the protamine-to-histone transition (Figure 5—figure supplement 2)
evidence: The claim is supported by microscopy data tracking protamine-GFP signal

claim: Both pronuclei recruit replication machinery in PEL embryos
source: Using antibodies against a replication protein (PCNA) and a kinetochore protein (Cenp-C), we also found that both pronuclei recruit replication machinery and initiate kinetochore assembly in PEL embryos (Figure 5—figure supplements 3, 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data showing PCNA localization

claim: Both pronuclei initiate kinetochore assembly in PEL embryos
source: Using antibodies against a replication protein (PCNA) and a kinetochore protein (Cenp-C), we also found that both pronuclei recruit replication machinery and initiate kinetochore assembly in PEL embryos (Figure 5—figure supplements 3, 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data showing Cenp-C localization

claim: The first visible sign of defects in PEL embryos was observed at metaphase
source: The first visible sign of defects in PEL embryos was observed at metaphase.
evidence: The claim is based on temporal analysis of embryo phenotypes

claim: Paternal DNA failed to condense synchronously with the maternal chromosomes in PEL embryos
source: We found that paternal DNA failed to condense synchronously with the maternal chromosomes in PEL embryos (Figure 5A,B).
evidence: The claim is supported by microscopy and quantitative circularity analysis

claim: In wild-type embryos, the ratio of paternal to maternal circularity was equal to one
source: In wild-type embryos, we found that the ratio of paternal to maternal circularity was equal to one, suggesting that both pronuclei undergo synchronous condensation.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative image analysis data

claim: Paternal DNA had twice the circularity of maternal DNA in PEL embryos
source: In contrast, paternal DNA had twice the circularity of maternal DNA in PEL embryos, suggesting asynchronous condensation due to failure of the paternal genome to compact into resolved chromatids in a timely fashion.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative image analysis data

claim: A prominent chromatin bridge enriched in paternal chromatin-specific AcH4 appeared in PEL embryos at the first anaphase
source: Immediately following this asynchronous metaphase in PEL embryos, we found that the paternal DNA failed to separate on the mitotic spindle. Specifically, a prominent chromatin bridge enriched in paternal chromatin-specific AcH4 appeared in PEL embryos at the first anaphase (Figure 5A, arrowhead, n = 20/20).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence microscopy data

claim: Only a fraction of the paternal genome mis-segregates in PEL embryos
source: We also observed AcH4 at the poles, suggesting that only a fraction of the paternal genome mis-segregates in PEL embryos.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation of AcH4 signal at both bridge and poles

claim: Defects in paternal chromatin organization are the primary source of mitotic arrest in embryos fathered by HP1E-depleted males
source: Based on these findings, we conclude that defects in paternal chromatin organization are the primary source of mitotic arrest in embryos fathered by HP1E-depleted males.
evidence: The claim is inferred from multiple lines of experimental evidence showing paternal chromatin defects

claim: Bypassing paternal chromatin participation fully rescues nuclear divisions in PEL embryos
source: We crossed the HP1E-depleted males to sesame females to ask whether bypassing paternal chromatin was sufficient to rescue mitotic cycling. We observed full rescue of nuclear divisions in these crosses (Figure 6A); the resulting embryos cycled maternal haploid nuclei identically to those 'fathered' by a wild-type male beyond embryonic cycle 12 (85% and 82%, respectively, p > 0.2, Figure 6A).
evidence: The claim is supported by genetic rescue experiment using sesame mutant females

claim: Defects in paternal chromatin dynamics are both necessary and sufficient to explain the mitotic arrest in PEL embryos sired by HP1E-depleted males
source: We therefore conclude that defects in paternal chromatin dynamics are both necessary and sufficient to explain the mitotic arrest in PEL embryos sired by HP1E-depleted males.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the sesame rescue experiment results

claim: HP1E protein is not detected in wild-type mature sperm head
source: We failed to detect HP1E protein cytologically in both wild-type mature sperm head (Figure 1D, Figure 1—figure supplement 3) and wild-type early embryos (data not shown).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence microscopy data

claim: HP1E protein is not detected in wild-type early embryos
source: We failed to detect HP1E protein cytologically in both wild-type mature sperm head (Figure 1D, Figure 1—figure supplement 3) and wild-type early embryos (data not shown).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence microscopy data

claim: Maternally deposited HP1E was unable to rescue the PEL defect associated with sperm from HP1E-depleted males
source: However, maternally deposited HP1E was unable to rescue the PEL defect associated with sperm from HP1E-depleted males (Figure 6B).
evidence: The claim is supported by genetic rescue experiment with maternal HP1E expression

claim: HP1E action during spermiogenesis, rather than in early embryogenesis, is responsible for ensuring proper embryonic mitosis
source: Consistent with the testis cytology presented in Figure 1, these data suggest that it is HP1E action during spermiogenesis, rather than in early embryogenesis, which is responsible for ensuring proper embryonic mitosis.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the failure of maternal HP1E to rescue and the localization data

claim: HP1E primes the paternal genome during spermiogenesis to ensure proper remodeling of the paternal genome in embryos post-fertilization
source: Combined with the successful rescue of mitotic cycling by sesame- mothers, we conclude that HP1E primes the paternal genome during spermiogenesis i.e., pre-fertilization, to ensure proper remodeling of the paternal genome in embryos post-fertilization.
evidence: The claim is inferred from multiple genetic experiments showing transgenerational effects

claim: The paternal Y was trapped as a bridge between nuclei in 94% of the male PEL embryos
source: We found that the paternal Y was trapped as a bridge between nuclei in 94% of the male PEL embryos (Figure 7B)
evidence: The claim is supported by FISH analysis data

claim: The maternal X was never found in the bridge in PEL embryos
source: We found that the paternal Y was trapped as a bridge between nuclei in 94% of the male PEL embryos (Figure 7B), whereas the maternal X was never found in the bridge (Figure 7B).
evidence: The claim is supported by FISH analysis data

claim: The paternal X-chromosome was trapped as a bridge in 60% of female PEL embryos
source: In female embryos, we found that the (inferred) maternal X-chromosome segregated faithfully while the (inferred) paternal X-chromosome was trapped as a bridge in 60% of embryos.
evidence: The claim is supported by FISH analysis data

claim: The large autosomes (chromosomes II and III) mis-segregated at only 4% and 15% frequency in male and female embryos, respectively
source: We found that the large autosomes—chromosomes II and III—mis-segregated at only 4% and 15% frequency in male and female embryos, respectively.
evidence: The claim is supported by FISH analysis data

claim: The dichotomy between sex chromosomes and the large autosomes in mis-segregation frequency is highly significant (p < 0.0001)
source: The dichotomy between sex chromosomes and the large autosomes is highly significant (p < 0.0001, Figure 7D).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of FISH data

claim: The paternal fourth chromosome mis-segregated at 25% frequency in female embryos
source: However, in female embryos, we found that the paternal fourth chromosome mis-segregated at 25% frequency, intermediate between the autosomes and sex chromosomes.
evidence: The claim is supported by FISH analysis data

claim: The Y-linked rDNA appears in the bridge at only 50% frequency in male PEL embryos
source: In male PEL embryos, we discovered the Y-linked rDNA in the bridge at only 50% frequency (Figure 8B, Figure 8D) compared to 95% frequency of the AATAC satellite probe (p < 0.0001).
evidence: The claim is supported by FISH analysis data with rDNA probes

claim: The AATAC satellite DNA or an immediately proximal satellite DNA cluster is in the telophase bridge in male embryos
source: Thus, it is the AATAC satellite DNA or an immediately proximal satellite DNA cluster that is in the telophase bridge in male embryos.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the differential frequencies of Y-rDNA vs AATAC satellite in bridges

claim: The X-linked rDNA locus in female PEL embryos occurs in the bridge at 85% frequency
source: In contrast, the X-linked rDNA locus in female PEL embryos occurs in the bridge at 85% frequency (Figure 7D, Figure 8B,D) compared to 60% for the 359 bp repeat (p < 0.02).
evidence: The claim is supported by FISH analysis data

claim: The DNA present in the telophase bridge is more likely to be proximal to the X-rDNA cluster than the 359 bp satellite repeats
source: These data suggest that the DNA present in the telophase bridge is more likely to be proximal to the X-rDNA cluster (although not the rDNA itself) than the 359 bp satellite repeats.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the differential frequencies of X-rDNA vs 359bp repeat in bridges

claim: HP1E action is required during sperm development to prime the paternal genome for embryonic chromosome segregation
source: Based on these findings, we conclude that HP1E action is required during sperm development to prime the paternal genome for embryonic chromosome segregation.
evidence: The claim is inferred from multiple lines of experimental evidence

claim: HP1E priming function is especially critical for faithful segregation of paternal sex chromosomes
source: This priming function is especially critical for faithful segregation of paternal sex chromosomes, which appear to be most vulnerable to HP1E depletion.
evidence: The claim is supported by FISH data showing enrichment of sex chromosomes in bridges

claim: No cell cycle checkpoint proteins have been identified to act in the very first embryonic mitotic cycle
source: No such cell cycle checkpoint proteins have been identified to act in the very first embryonic mitotic cycle (O'Farrell et al., 2004)
evidence: The claim cites a previous publication as support

claim: HP1E encodes a novel function that ensures paternal genome stability in the embryo
source: We found that HP1E encodes a novel function that ensures paternal genome stability in the embryo.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the functional characterization experiments

claim: HP1E is developmentally restricted within the male germline
source: Our cytological and transcriptome analysis revealed that HP1E is developmentally restricted within the male germline, where it contributes to heterochromatin integrity.
evidence: The claim is supported by localization and expression data

claim: HP1E contributes to heterochromatin integrity in the male germline
source: Our cytological and transcriptome analysis revealed that HP1E is developmentally restricted within the male germline, where it contributes to heterochromatin integrity.
evidence: The claim is inferred from RNA-seq data showing heterochromatin gene misregulation

claim: HP1E depletion during sperm development results in paternal chromosomes failing to condense in synchrony with the maternal chromosomes
source: HP1E depletion during sperm development results in a highly penetrant PEL phenotype in which paternal chromosomes, especially the paternal sex chromosomes, fail to condense in synchrony with the maternal chromosomes and ultimately cause mitotic catastrophe.
evidence: The claim is supported by microscopy and quantitative analysis data

claim: The PEL embryonic phenotype could not be rescued by egg-supplied HP1E
source: We further showed that the PEL embryonic phenotype could not be rescued by egg-supplied HP1E but could be rescued if the paternal DNA was excluded from participating in embryonic mitosis.
evidence: The claim is supported by maternal rescue experiment data

claim: The PEL embryonic phenotype could be rescued if the paternal DNA was excluded from participating in embryonic mitosis
source: We further showed that the PEL embryonic phenotype could not be rescued by egg-supplied HP1E but could be rescued if the paternal DNA was excluded from participating in embryonic mitosis.
evidence: The claim is supported by sesame rescue experiment data

claim: HP1E acts pre-fertilization to ensure proper chromosome condensation and segregation of paternal chromosomes post-fertilization
source: These observations support a model (Figure 9A) under which HP1E acts pre-fertilization to ensure proper chromosome condensation and segregation of paternal chromosomes post-fertilization.
evidence: The claim is inferred from multiple experimental results showing transgenerational effects

claim: The 'hit and run' priming function clearly distinguishes HP1E from all other previously characterized paternal effect lethal genes
source: The 'hit and run' priming function clearly distinguishes HP1E from all other previously characterized paternal effect lethal genes, which encode proteins that are transmitted to the embryo via sperm (Browning and Strome, 1996; Fitch and Wakimoto, 1998; Fitch et al., 1998; Loppin et al., 2005b; Smith and Wakimoto, 2007; Gao et al., 2011; Seidel et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim compares HP1E to other PEL genes described in cited literature

claim: The HP1E-depletion phenotype is reminiscent of Drosophila fathers infected with Wolbachia bacteria crossed to uninfected females
source: The HP1E-depletion phenotype is instead reminiscent of Drosophila fathers infected with Wolbachia bacteria crossed to uninfected females (Serbus et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim compares HP1E phenotype to Wolbachia-induced phenotype from cited literature

claim: Wolbachia-associated PEL results in mis-segregation of the entire paternal genome
source: However, Wolbachia-associated PEL results in mis-segregation of the entire paternal genome (Landmann et al., 2009) rather than just the heterochromatin-rich chromosomes observed in HP1E—PEL (Figure 5A, Figure 7B).
evidence: The claim contrasts HP1E phenotype with Wolbachia phenotype from cited literature

claim: The HP1E PEL defect is completely independent of Wolbachia
source: Moreover, the HP1E PEL defect is completely independent of Wolbachia (we find that PEL phenotype persists for Wolbachia-free males and females).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data using Wolbachia-free flies

claim: HP1E supports a novel chromatin requirement to prime paternally inherited genomes for synchronous and successful embryonic mitosis
source: We therefore conclude that HP1E supports a novel chromatin requirement to prime paternally inherited genomes for synchronous and successful embryonic mitosis.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the unique characteristics of HP1E function

claim: HP1E depletion results in the global up-regulation of heterochromatin-embedded genes
source: However, our finding that HP1E depletion results in the global up-regulation of heterochromatin-embedded genes, together with our observation that the heterochromatin-rich paternal sex chromosomes are most vulnerable to HP1E depletion, lead us to favor the alternate model that HP1E functions as a canonical HP1 protein during spermiogenesis.
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq data

claim: HP1E functions as a canonical HP1 protein during spermiogenesis
source: However, our finding that HP1E depletion results in the global up-regulation of heterochromatin-embedded genes, together with our observation that the heterochromatin-rich paternal sex chromosomes are most vulnerable to HP1E depletion, lead us to favor the alternate model that HP1E functions as a canonical HP1 protein during spermiogenesis.
evidence: The claim is inferred from RNA-seq and FISH data patterns

claim: Large stretches of uninterrupted heterochromatic DNA pose a unique challenge to replication
source: Indeed, large stretches of uninterrupted heterochromatic DNA, as found on the Drosophila sex chromosomes, pose a unique challenge to replication (Leach et al., 2000) (Pryor et al., 1980; Collins et al., 2002).
evidence: The claim cites previous publications as support

claim: HP1A is essential for embryo viability
source: Previous studies have shown that HP1A is essential for embryo viability (Eissenberg et al., 1992).
evidence: The claim cites a previous publication as support

claim: Paternally-acting HP1E is essential for embryogenesis
source: We show here that paternally-acting HP1E is also essential for embryogenesis.
evidence: The claim is supported by the PEL phenotype data

claim: Both HP1A and HP1E evolve under purifying selection
source: Both HP1A and HP1E evolve under purifying selection (Levine et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim cites a previous publication as support

claim: HP1E has been recurrently lost over evolutionary time
source: Despite ancient origins, HP1E has been recurrently lost over evolutionary time.
evidence: The claim is based on phylogenomic analysis

claim: HP1E has been apparently replaced by younger, testis restricted HP1 paralogs on at least two occasions during Drosophila evolution
source: HP1E has been apparently replaced by younger, testis restricted HP1 paralogs on at least two occasions during Drosophila evolution (Levine et al., 2012) (Figure 9—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim cites a previous publication and is supported by phylogenetic data

claim: Drosophila pseudoobscura and related species encode neither HP1E nor a putative replacement testis-specific HP1 gene
source: Curiously, Drosophila pseudoobscura and related species encode neither HP1E nor a putative replacement testis-specific HP1 gene.
evidence: The claim is based on phylogenomic analysis

claim: HP1E loss in D. pseudoobscura-related species occurred during the same 7-million evolutionary period as a major sex chromosome rearrangement event
source: We previously found that HP1E loss along in D. pseudoobscura-related species occurred during the same 7-million evolutionary period as a major sex chromosome rearrangement event (Levine et al., 2012), in which the ancestral Y was lost, a neo-Y chromosome was born, and the ancestral X fused to an autosome (Carvalho and Clark, 2005; Larracuente et al., 2010) (Figure 8B).
evidence: The claim cites previous publications as support

claim: Karyotypic changes can bring distal heterochromatin into closer proximity to euchromatin
source: Such karyotypic changes can bring distal heterochromatin into closer proximity to euchromatin and be sufficient to alter heterochromatin packaging (Spofford, 1976), replication timing (Abramov et al., 2005) or even delete blocks of satellite repeats (Garagna et al., 1995).
evidence: The claim cites previous publications as support

claim: Heterochromatin evolution via chromosomal rearrangements may have obviated maintenance of HP1E's essential heterochromatin function, leading to its degeneration in D. pseudoobscura
source: Thus, heterochromatin evolution via chromosomal rearrangements may have obviated maintenance of HP1E's essential heterochromatin function, leading to its degeneration in D. pseudoobscura.
evidence: The claim is speculative reasoning based on evolutionary patterns

claim: The only other characterized PEL gene that supports paternal chromatin function in Drosophila embryos, k81, is lineage-restricted despite being essential for paternal telomere function
source: Intriguingly, the only other characterized PEL gene that supports paternal chromatin function in Drosophila embryos, k81, is similarly lineage-restricted despite being essential for paternal telomere function (Dubruille et al., 2010; Gao et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim cites previous publications as support

claim: Maternally deposited proteins required for paternal chromatin reorganization following fertilization are generally conserved from fly to human
source: In contrast, maternally deposited proteins required for paternal chromatin reorganization following fertilization are generally conserved from fly to human (e.g., Loppin et al., 2005a; Konev et al., 2007; Delabaere et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim cites previous publications as support

claim: The essential functions of paternal control of DNA deposition and chromatin remodeling for embryonic mitosis are likely to be conserved in most animals
source: It specifically suggests that even though the essential functions of paternal control of DNA deposition and chromatin remodeling for embryonic mitosis are likely to be conserved in most animals, whereas the identity of those genes is not.
evidence: The claim is speculative reasoning based on evolutionary patterns

claim: Young genes can rapidly acquire essential chromatin functions due to dynamic chromatin evolution
source: Not only can young genes rapidly acquire essential chromatin functions due to dynamic chromatin evolution (Chen et al., 2010; Ross et al., 2013)
evidence: The claim cites previous publications as support

claim: Chromatin changes driven by karyotype evolution may drive the extinction of ancient genes encoding once-essential functions
source: but chromatin changes, such as those driven by karyotype evolution, may also drive the extinction of ancient genes encoding once-essential functions (Drinnenberg et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim cites a previous publication as support

claim: Faithful chromosome segregation requires careful orchestration of chromosomal condensation, alignment, and movement of mitotic chromosomes during every eukaryotic cell division
source: Faithful chromosome segregation requires careful orchestration of chromosomal condensation, alignment, and movement of mitotic chromosomes during every eukaryotic cell division (Rhind and Russell, 2012).
evidence: The claim cites a previous publication as support for established knowledge

claim: The very first embryonic mitosis in animals requires additional synchronization beyond typical mitotic requirements
source: The very first embryonic mitosis in animals requires additional synchronization.
evidence: The claim is based on established biological knowledge

claim: Paternally and maternally inherited genomes undergo independent chromatin reorganization and replication prior to mitotic entry
source: Paternally and maternally inherited genomes undergo independent chromatin reorganization and replication prior to mitotic entry.
evidence: The claim is based on established biological knowledge

claim: Maternal chromosomes must complete meiosis and then transition from a meiotic conformation to an interphase-like state in preparation for replication
source: For instance, maternal chromosomes must complete meiosis (Sen et al., 2013) and then transition from a meiotic conformation to an interphase-like state in preparation for replication.
evidence: The claim cites a previous publication as support

claim: The sperm-deposited, paternal chromosomes must undergo a radical transition from a highly compact, protamine-rich state to a decondensed, histone-rich state before DNA replication
source: The sperm-deposited, paternal chromosomes must undergo an even more radical transition from a highly compact, protamine-rich state to a decondensed, histone-rich state before DNA replication (Braun, 2001; Miller et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim cites previous publications as support

claim: Maternal and paternal genomes synchronously enter the first mitosis despite divergent requirements to achieve replication- and mitotic-competency
source: Despite these divergent requirements to achieve replication- and mitotic-competency, maternal and paternal genomes synchronously enter the first mitosis.
evidence: The claim is based on established biological knowledge

claim: Failure to carry out paternal chromosome remodeling in a timely fashion results in paternal genome loss and embryonic inviability
source: Failure to carry out paternal chromosome remodeling in a timely fashion results in paternal genome loss and embryonic inviability (Loppin et al., 2001; McLay and Clarke, 2003; Landmann et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim cites previous publications as support

claim: The transition from a protamine-rich sperm nucleus to a competent paternal pronucleus requires the action of numerous maternally deposited proteins in the egg
source: The transition from a protamine-rich sperm nucleus to a competent paternal pronucleus requires the action of numerous maternally deposited proteins in the egg (McLay and Clarke, 2003).
evidence: The claim cites a previous publication as support

claim: Paternal genome decondensation post-fertilization requires the integration of histone H3.3
source: For instance, paternal genome decondensation post-fertilization requires the integration of histone H3.3, a histone variant deposited by the maternal proteins HIRA (Loppin et al., 2005a), CHD1 (Konev et al., 2007), and Yemanuclein (Orsi et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim cites previous publications as support

claim: Maternally-deposited MH/Spartan protein localizes exclusively to the replicating paternal genome and is required for faithful paternal chromosome segregation during the first embryonic division
source: Similarly, maternally-deposited MH/Spartan protein localizes exclusively to the replicating paternal genome and is required for faithful paternal chromosome segregation during the first embryonic division (Delabaere et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim cites a previous publication as support

claim: Only a handful of PEL genes have been characterized in animals
source: Only a handful of PEL genes have been characterized in animals (Browning and Strome, 1996; Fitch and Wakimoto, 1998; Fitch et al., 1998; Loppin et al., 2005b; Smith and Wakimoto, 2007; Gao et al., 2011; Seidel et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim cites previous publications as support

claim: The sperm-inherited K81 protein localizes exclusively to paternal chromosome termini and ensures telomere integrity
source: Only one of these PEL proteins directly localizes to paternal chromosomes; the sperm-inherited K81 protein localizes exclusively to paternal chromosome termini and ensures telomere integrity (Dubruille et al., 2010; Gao et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim cites previous publications as support

claim: Wolbachia infects more than 50% of insect species
source: The notion that maternal control is sufficient to accomplish paternal genome remodeling is challenged by recent findings from the intracellular Wolbachia bacterium that infects more than 50% of insect species (Hilgenboecker et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim cites a previous publication as support

claim: Wolbachia-infected Drosophila males mated to uninfected females father embryos that arrest soon after the first zygotic mitosis
source: Wolbachia-infected Drosophila males mated to uninfected females father embryos that arrest soon after the first zygotic mitosis (Lassy and Karr, 1996).
evidence: The claim cites a previous publication as support

claim: In Wolbachia-induced embryonic arrest, paternal genomes enter the first mitosis with unresolved sister chromatids that fail to separate on the mitotic spindle
source: Embryonic arrest occurs because paternal genomes enter the first mitosis with unresolved sister chromatids that fail to separate on the mitotic spindle (Callaini et al., 1997; Landmann et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim cites previous publications as support

claim: HP1 proteins are defined by a combination of a chromodomain that mediates protein-histone interactions and a chromoshadow domain that mediates protein–protein interactions
source: HP1 proteins are defined as such by a combination of two domains—a chromodomain that mediates protein-histone interactions and a chromoshadow domain that mediates protein–protein interactions (Aasland and Stewart, 1995; Eissenberg and Elgin, 2000).
evidence: The claim cites previous publications as support for established knowledge

claim: HP1 proteins orchestrate genome-wide chromosomal organization in plants, animals, fungi, and some protists
source: To investigate the potential for paternal control over sperm genome remodeling post-fertilization, we took a candidate gene approach, focusing on the Heterochromatin Protein 1 (HP1) proteins that orchestrate genome-wide chromosomal organization in plants, animals, fungi, and some protists (Lomberk et al., 2006).
